passage: Looking back at last term, I think I was the one doing the pushing, not the one being pushed. I'd decided to skip maths tuition every Thursday to hang out at the arcade. I hadn't told Abba, and every Thursday my stomach churned on the walk there. So I started on Harsha. "Come on, one day. Don't be a baby. Everyone skips." I said it again and again, louder each week. When Harsha finally said, "Fine, just this once," I felt a rush, like I'd won something. That should have told me something. Honestly, it wasn't about Harsha at all. If Harsha came, I wasn't the only one breaking the rule, or the only one who'd get caught. And for a second I felt big instead of scared. The next Thursday Harsha said no, quietly, and walked into tuition. I stood outside for a minute, then followed. I, Farhan, still haven't said why I pushed so hard. Maybe I'll start with this.

qa.q: Where did Farhan go instead of maths tuition?
qa.a: To hang out at the arcade.

qa.q: Why did Farhan push Harsha so hard?
qa.a: Farhan felt scared and alone in the risky choice; getting Harsha to join meant not being the only one, and for a second Farhan felt big instead of scared.

qa.q: What could Farhan do now?
qa.a: Farhan could tell Harsha honestly why the pushing happened and apologise, and talk to Abba about the skipped Thursdays.

qa.q: How might Harsha have felt being called a baby each week?
qa.a: Harsha likely felt pressured and small, which is why the “fine, just this once” came, before a quiet no the next week.

grounding: Shows a teenager pressing a friend to join a risky choice to feel less alone and more powerful, driven by the pusher's own uncertainty.

passage: Jyoti, sit, before you go to that bank tomorrow. When I was twenty-four and had just started teaching, I went to a bank to open a savings account. The man at the counter smiled, called me madam, and said, "Today only, you can add this plan, very good for your future." Then he spoke fast: premium, lock-in, surrender value, riders. I understood maybe one word in five. There were people behind me in the queue. I felt so small, so embarrassed to ask what any of it meant in front of everyone. He had the pen open, pointing at the line. And I signed. Years later I learned my money was stuck in something I didn't want and couldn't leave without losing a lot. What I should have done was the thing I was most shy to do: say, I'll take the papers home and come back. That rushed feeling, the shame of asking? That's exactly when to stop. Your Rukmini Ammamma learned it the costly way.

qa.q: Which words did the man use that Rukmini didn't understand?
qa.a: Premium, lock-in, surrender value and riders.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel at the counter?
qa.a: Rukmini felt small and embarrassed to ask what the words meant, rushed by the queue and the open pen.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what would have helped?
qa.a: The moment of signing; taking the papers home and coming back after understanding them would have given time to ask and decide.

qa.q: Why might the man at the counter have been in such a hurry?
qa.a: He may have been under pressure to sell the plan, so a quick signature served him more than Rukmini's understanding did.

grounding: Shows a young adult at a bank counter pushed to sign on the spot with jargon she did not follow, too embarrassed to ask.

passage: By four o'clock Lavanya had knocked on nineteen doors in Karimganj and sold nothing. Her target for the month was twelve water purifiers; she had four. Arnab, her area manager, had texted twice: "Push harder. Say the offer ends today." At the twentieth house, an elderly couple invited her in for tea. Lavanya smiled her brightest smile, called the woman Mashi, admired her garden. The words came out smoothly: "Only today, this price. Tomorrow it goes up." It wasn't true; the price had been the same for months. The old man reached for his wallet. Lavanya felt her cheeks go hot. She did believe in the purifier; her own family used one. But the lie sat heavy in her throat. "Actually, Mesho," she said, "the price will be the same next week too. Talk to your son first." They didn't buy that day. Walking back to the bus stand, she wondered what she would tell Arnab.

qa.q: How many purifiers had Lavanya sold against her target of twelve?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: How did Lavanya feel after saying the offer ended today?
qa.a: Lavanya felt ashamed, her cheeks hot and the lie heavy in her throat, even though she believed in the purifier.

qa.q: What would you advise buyers dealing with a very friendly seller?
qa.a: Judge what the seller does, not the warmth: check whether a today-only claim is true, and take time to talk to family before buying.

qa.q: How might the elderly couple see Lavanya's correction?
qa.a: They may feel respected and trust her more, since she told them the truth even though it cost her a sale.

grounding: Shows a salesperson under targets using urgency and warmth, who believes in the product but catches herself bending the truth.

subtype: Sleep on it and read it [Response]
passage: At the tractor dealer's tent at the Sonpur fair, the salesman slid a form across the table. "Only for fair days, Yogesh-bhai. Sign today and the rotavator comes free." Yogesh turned the pen over in his fingers. The man was friendly and the machine was shiny, but half the terms were printed so small he'd need Usha's reading glasses. "Give me all the terms in writing," he said. "I'll come back tomorrow." The salesman's smile thinned. "Tomorrow maybe the offer is gone." "Then it wasn't much of an offer." That night, under the lantern, Usha read every line aloud. The interest was higher than he'd been told, and the free rotavator had a charge buried on page three. Next morning they went to the cooperative society office and to another dealer at the far end of the fair, and compared. Yogesh walked past the first tent without stopping. The salesman called out a new, lower price. Yogesh just waved.

qa.q: What did the salesman say would come free if Yogesh signed today?
qa.a: The rotavator.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling as he turned the pen in his fingers?
qa.a: Yogesh felt tempted by the shiny machine but uneasy and cautious about the tiny print he couldn't read.

qa.q: Which steps protected Yogesh?
qa.a: Asking for all the terms in writing, waiting a night, having Usha read every line, and comparing with the cooperative and another dealer before deciding.

qa.q: What does the salesman's new, lower price suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the fair-days deadline was pressure rather than a real limit, and that the salesman still wanted the sale.

grounding: Shows a buyer who waits a day, asks for the terms in writing, compares alternatives and walks away from pressure.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 2, Friday.
At show-and-tell, Dilnaz brought an empty snack packet with a cartoon tiger on it. She said, "If you eat these, you get lots of friends, like in the video." Three others nodded; they had seen the same advert. When I asked what the video was for, Dilnaz said it was "a story about the tiger".
I didn't laugh. We looked at two adverts together on the smartboard and talked about who made them and why: to make us want to buy. Dilnaz asked, "So the tiger doesn't give real friends?" I said friends come from playing together, not from a packet. She thought about it, then asked Meenu to play tag.
I will send a short note home suggesting parents talk about adverts too.
Pallavi

qa.q: What did Dilnaz bring to show-and-tell?
qa.a: An empty snack packet with a cartoon tiger on it.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz believe the snack would bring?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt hopeful and sure that eating it would bring lots of friends, and thought the advert was a story about the tiger.

qa.q: How did Pallavi help the children understand adverts?
qa.a: Pallavi didn't laugh; the class looked at two adverts, talked about who made them and why, and heard that friends come from playing together.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's parents help at home?
qa.a: They could talk about adverts while watching together, so Dilnaz learns to ask who made them and why.

grounding: Shows a young child believing an advert means a snack brings friends, not yet able to tell an ad from a story, and an adult explaining.

subtype: Trusting an influencer like a friend [Receiver]
passage: Okay, Bidisha, promise you won't laugh. You know that creator I watch every night, Tuki Plays? I've watched him for two years. He says "good night, fam" at the end of every stream, and he remembers the regulars' names. He said my name once. Mine! It felt like he was a big brother. So when he said, "Guys, this headset changed my life, link below," I didn't even think. I saved my birthday money and bought it. It's fine, honestly. Just fine. Then last week my cousin showed me the tiny line under his video: paid partnership. And the month before, he'd called a different headset "the only one I trust". I felt so stupid. Not because of the money, but because I'd thought he was talking to me like a friend, when he was also doing his job. I still watch him. But now I check for that line first. I'm Darshan, and I'm officially a sceptic.

qa.q: What line did Darshan's cousin point out under the video?
qa.a: Paid partnership.

qa.q: Why did Darshan feel stupid?
qa.a: Darshan felt embarrassed and a bit betrayed, having trusted the creator like a big brother without seeing that the recommendation was paid.

qa.q: What habit has Darshan started, and why does it help?
qa.a: Checking for the paid-partnership line first, which is a reminder that a friendly voice can still be selling.

qa.q: How might Tuki Plays see the recommendations?
qa.a: To the creator it may simply be paid work alongside the streams, even if viewers like Darshan hear it as a friend's advice.

grounding: Shows a teenager who trusted a creator like a friend and bought a recommended headset without seeing the post was paid.

passage: It was 1 a.m. in exam week, and Minakshi should have been revising microbiology. Instead she was scrolling. A girl her age on a rooftop in Goa, skin glowing, captioned "my morning routine". Then an ad: "Tired of dull skin? Our 5-step glow kit, 40% off tonight." Then another girl, another beach. Minakshi caught her reflection in the dark screen: spots from stress, hair tied with a rubber band. Everyone else seemed to have their lives sorted. She had just enough money left for the month's bus pass, and her thumb hovered over Buy now. Zainab, her flatmate, padded in for water and saw the screen. "That one," she said, tapping the rooftop girl. "I follow her too. She posted last month that she uses three filters and a ring light. And the kit company pays her." Minakshi laughed, a little shakily. She closed the app, put the phone face down, and opened her microbiology notes.

qa.q: What did the ad offer?
qa.a: A 5-step glow kit, 40% off tonight.

qa.q: How was Minakshi feeling while scrolling?
qa.a: Minakshi felt behind and insecure, comparing her stress spots and rubber-band hair with glowing, sorted lives.

qa.q: What helped Minakshi step back?
qa.a: Zainab pointed out the filters, the ring light and the paid deal, which showed the polished image was edited and selling; Minakshi then closed the app.

qa.q: How might Zainab see these posts?
qa.a: Zainab sees them with a clearer eye, knowing about filters and sponsorship, and wants to protect Minakshi from buying out of insecurity.

grounding: Shows a young adult comparing herself with edited photos and ads for glowing skin late at night, with the product sold as the answer.

subtype: Asking who pays and what is left out [Response]
passage: In the office pantry, Indu held out her phone to Pranav. "This guy's course will fix your career in thirty days. Everyone on my feed is doing it." Pranav watched the clip: a man in a sunlit flat, laptop open, a speedboat behind him, saying, "If you're stuck in a nine-to-five, you're wasting your life." Pranav smiled; it was a good video. Then he scrolled to the caption. Small grey letters: Sponsored. He searched the course name plus "review" and skipped the first page of glowing posts. On a forum, people wrote that the lessons were free videos repackaged. "So what is he actually selling?" Pranav said. "A course. But first he's selling the feeling that my job is a waste." Indu frowned. "Is it, though?" "Some days," Pranav laughed. "But I didn't think so till I saw the speedboat." He put the kettle on. "Nice video, though. I'll just keep my money."

qa.q: What small grey word appeared in the caption?
qa.a: Sponsored.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling as he watched the clip?
qa.a: Pranav enjoyed it, smiling at a good video, while staying curious and sceptical about who had paid for it.

qa.q: Which checks did Pranav use?
qa.a: He looked for the sponsored label, searched for independent reviews beyond the first glowing page, and noticed the need the ad was trying to create.

qa.q: How might Indu feel after Pranav's comments?
qa.a: Indu seems unsettled, asking whether it is a waste, perhaps wondering if the ad had made her doubt her own job too.

grounding: Shows an adult checking whether a post is sponsored, looking for independent reviews and noticing the need the ad creates, while still enjoying it.
